did.abstract: The collection is comprised of correspondence, records, ephemera, photographs, realia, maps, and other materials created by, or related to, the American Oriental Society (AOS). Materials span from the Society's founding in 1842 to 2012 and document the establishment, collecting, and business functions of the AOS. The collection's strength lies in the development of the Near East and Asia as an area of study for 19th and early 20th century American scholars found in the extensive correspondence, manuscripts, and publications of the collection. Taken together, the historic and modern records provide a comprehensive look at how the AOS was founded, the people involved in its establishment, the networks developed with scholars and researchers, and how the Society evolved over time.

custodhist.head: Custodial History
custodhist.p: Materials for the archival collection were previously housed in Yale's Sterling Memorial Library, as part of the Society's library. The American Oriental Society library was maintained by the Society's librarian. In 2016, the archival collection was identified and separated from the rest of the library's holdings. In 2024 the archive was gifted to Yale's Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The collection is comprised of correspondence, records, ephemera, photographs, realia, maps, and other materials created by, or related to, the American Oriental Society (AOS). Materials span from the Society's founding in 1842 to 2012 and document the establishment, collecting, and business functions of the AOS. The collection's strength lies in the development of the Near East and Asia as an area of study for 19th and early 20th century American scholars found in the extensive correspondence, manuscripts, and publications of the collection. Taken together, the historic and modern records provide a comprehensive look at how the AOS was founded, the people involved in its establishment, the networks developed with scholars and researchers, and how the Society evolved over time.

The Society's historic records (primarily 1850-1930) include: annual meeting proceedings and reports; board of directors meeting minutes; correspondence with and records of various Society officers (Albert T. Clay, Maurice Bloomfield, Edward Salisbury, Charles Ogden, John C. Archer); copies of incoming and outgoing correspondence; manuscripts collected by the Society; catalog and lists of library books; vouchers, ledgers, and records of the treasurer; photographs of Society dinners and members; manuscripts collected by the Society; topical scrapbooks that contain photographs, readings, clippings, and notes; and stamps and typesets.

The Society's modern records (primarily 1930-1985) include: correspondence; membership applications, lists, and correspondence; records for the Executive Committee and Board of Directors; investments and treasurer's records; records relating to the Journal of the American Oriental Society; contracts, sales, copyright, and correspondence relating to monographs; American Council of Learned Societies correspondence and reports; annual meeting correspondence and records; records of the journal editors; records of AOS branches. The materials are arranged and identified by distinct record groups and mostly pertain to the routine business functions of the AOS.

The division between the historic and modern records approximately corresponds to the reorganization of the Society in 1936 in which it adopted a formal records management structure and subsequently retained its records according to established record groups.

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: The American Oriental Society (AOS) was founded in 1842 in Boston, Massachusetts and is still active today. It is a learned society dedicated to the study of languages and literature of the Near East and Asia, covering subjects such as philology, literary criticism, textual criticism, paleography, epigraphy, linguistics, biography, religion, philosophy, folklore, and art. The AOS has close ties to Yale University and Yale University Library, which has stewarded the Society's library since 1855. In 2025 the AOS changed its name to the American Society for Premodern Asia. The Society publishes the Journal of the American Society for Premodern Asia (previously the Journal of the American Oriental Society ), which is a quarterly publication that seeks to advance the scholarship and research of specialists in West, Central, South, and East Asian literatures, languages, and civilizations.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The series contains routine business records approximately from the founding of the society until 1936, when a formal record management structure was adopted. It includes correspondence; meeting proceedings; manuscripts submitted to the Society for publication in its journal; records of its library's holdings, including shelf lists and catalog; and objects and photographs.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series is organized into seven subseries: Administrative; Correspondence; Membership; Executive committee; Objects and photographs; Financial; Journal; Manuscripts; Library; and Annual meeting. Materials are arranged chronologically therein except where specified.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This series pertains to the routine business functions of the Society (mostly 1936-2012): correspondence; membership applications and lists; records of its committees, editors, and branches; and records of sales and copyright of its publications.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The series is arranged into eleven sub-series that reflect the original records management structure established by the Society in 1936: 1. Correspondence; 2. Membership; 3. Executive committee; 4. Investments; 5. Treasurer's reports; 6. Journal; 7. Monographs; 8. American Council of Learned Societies; 9. Annual meeting; 10. Editors; and 11. American Oriental Society branches.
